compression.title: Labor Notes
compression.lede: is a media and organizing project and a network of rank-and-file members, local union leaders and labor activists, published since 1979 as the monthly magazine of the same name by the Labor Education and Research Project (its pages; Wikipedia; maryleelabor record); as an independent publication it prints the voices who say the movement "could be doing better" (About).

sentences.text: Labor Notes is, on its own home page, "a media and organizing project that has been the voice of union activists who want to put the movement back in the labor movement since 1979" (labornotes.org), which the maryleelabor census record enters as "a media and organizing project: monthly magazine, website, books, conferences and workshops, and a network of rank-and-file members, local union leaders and labor activists" and tags "NOT a union" (maryleelabor record).

Wikipedia enters it as the magazine, "a monthly magazine that supports union organizing and collective bargaining in the United States", first issued in March 1979 and published by the Labor Education and Research Project, "an American non-profit organization and network for rank-and-file union members and grassroots labor activists" (Wikipedia), the name its site's footer gives as copyright holder, "© 2005-2023", and the census as its other name (labornotes.org; maryleelabor record).

The census asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", files it under movement documents, worker power and labor action, with a periodical run and an organizing resource as its evidence and an article, a book or pamphlet, a conference or a Troublemakers School as its unit, and gives its object as union and workplace struggles told from the side of union activists and rank-and-file members since 1979 (maryleelabor record).

Wikipedia dates its launch to the aftermath of the Bituminous Coal Strike of 1977–1978 and "the cross-union solidarity it generated", and places it in Detroit, Michigan, with an East Coast office in Brooklyn, New York (Wikipedia); its own footer gives a Brooklyn mailing address, its X profile gives Detroit, MI, and one card on the rail carries only the title "Labor Notes | Brooklyn NY" (labornotes.org; Labor Notes on X).

In Wikipedia's history it held its first conference, Organizing Against Concessions, in 1982 and published Jane Slaughter's Concessions and How to Beat Them in 1983, a sentence the article marks as needing a citation; it opposed NAFTA and in 1992 published Unions and Free Trade by Kim Moody and Mary McGinn; and it brought the leaders of immigrant worker centers together at its conference (Wikipedia).

The census records 1979 as its founding and 1979 to the present as its period, the United States mainly, with workers' struggles abroad (maryleelabor record), and a participant writing in the Metro DC DSA's Washington Socialist calls it "a nonprofit organization founded in 1979 as a publication and movement hub" for rank-and-file union members, in a publication whose content "does not necessarily reflect the views of Metro DC DSA or the national DSA" (Washington Socialist, summer 2024).

Through its magazine, website, books, conferences and workshops it promotes "organizing, aggressive strategies to take on employers, labor-community solidarity, and unions that are run by their members", and it is "also a network of rank-and-file members, local union leaders, and labor activists" that encourages connections between workers across unions, worker centers, industries and countries "from the bottom up" (labornotes.org/about); Wikipedia has it promote a revitalization of the labor movement "through social movement unionism and union democracy" (Wikipedia).

Its about page states the position it holds: "For the most part, our leaders are doing a poor job of navigating us through the crisis," some unable to "get beyond business-as-usual" and others not believing "that workers themselves need to have a say in their unions", and it exists, with 45 years of movement building behind it, as a resource for those who want to "chart a new course for the labor movement" (labornotes.org/about); the census records it as keeping "the voice of union activists and rank-and-file members, including their critique of union leaderships", and tags it "NOT a neutral record of labor" (maryleelabor record).

It is "best known for our monthly magazine of the same name", which reports news about workers "from workers’ point of view" (labornotes.org/about) and is sold at "$30 for 11 issues" (labornotes.org), a magazine its subscription page says has for four decades offered activists "a ringside view of labor's ups and downs" on struggles "across the street or around the world" (Labor Notes subscription page), its articles free online (maryleelabor record).

Its pages carry argument as well as report: in a roundtable series on how unions can defend worker power against Trump 2.0, Kate Bronfenbrenner argues that "unions must organize workers in the nation’s largest and most powerful corporations" without waiting for labor law reform (Labor Notes, 22 October 2025).

The about page gives the condition on which it prints criticism of leaderships: "And as an independent publication, we’re free to include the voices who say we could be doing better—and tell how." (labornotes.org/about).

The archive's report on the left's lost capacity for internal critique finds that "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender", its cases including the SPD, where the revisionist critique, condemned without expulsion of the critic, "kept its organ", and the New Reasoner, whose critique "kept an organ and found a wider field" (#1725).

Among the six conditions under which that report finds critique turned into voice, "the leadership did not monopolize communication" (#1725); Rex Fraction's field manual reads the same need in labor's own history, unions that organized through company-controlled channels finding them "shut down the moment organizing became effective", so that "building independent media, union halls, alternative communication networks" was "costly and slow but structurally necessary" (#499).

The census reads Labor Notes as "an organ independent of the union executives it criticizes, of the kind #1725 finds holding critique: a publication, a network and a conference through which a rank-and-file position keeps being stated and can be taken up later", existing in its own terms to "put the movement back in the labor movement" (maryleelabor record; labornotes.org).

It is held as an independent publication supported by subscriptions, book sales and tax-deductible donations, with hundreds of supporters giving monthly, and it asks that reprints "credit both the author and Labor Notes" and link to the original story online (labornotes.org/about), terms the census records as a reprint policy with no licence stated (maryleelabor record).

Wikipedia has it work "to bridge the gap between isolated rank-and-file caucuses and reform groups", the most notable example being Teamsters for a Democratic Union (Wikipedia), and #1725 counts TDU, from 1976, among the counter-cases in which critique acquired power, its strategy "to build a constituency able to replace officials, without depending on their willingness to be persuaded", taken from the organization's own history and "unchecked independently here", all of them running on one mechanism by which "critics associate independently, form a constituency, and hold a route from opposition into decision-making power" (#1725).
The report keeps its limit on those cases: "these are unions and a movement, which are different things from ideological parties, and what carries across is the mechanism" (#1725).

On 31 October 2026 its home page led with "Members Alarmed by End-Run around Democracy at Buffalo Health Care Local" (29 October 2026), "State Workers Strike Across California" and "UFCW Members Protect Local Election After Sham Merger Attempt" (labornotes.org), and its X account carried an insurgent slate challenging longtime incumbents in UFCW Local 8-Golden State and a founding member of the IATSE CREW reform caucus saying that "someone from Labor Notes is going to be there to pick you up" (Labor Notes on X).

The census finds the losing side kept as its sources show, in an independent publication that prints criticism of union leaders and in current stories of members contesting their own locals, and records that "Whether it keeps the record of positions after they lose is not shown in the saved pages"; it lists among what the resource does not answer counts of strikes, members or campaigns and the account given by the leaderships it criticizes, except as its stories report them (maryleelabor record).

Every two years it holds a national conference that "attracts thousands of activists, about a tenth of them from other countries" (labornotes.org/about), by Wikipedia's count more than a thousand union members and leaders from the United States, Canada, Mexico and other countries meeting "to help activists build networks based on shared issues" (Wikipedia); its 2024 page calls these "the biggest gatherings of grassroots union activists, union reformers, and all-around troublemakers out there" and puts face-to-face meetings, union and caucus meetings among them, at their heart (labornotes.org/2024).

The 2022 conference brought some 4,000 to Chicago, its main sessions livestreamed and kept as video (Labor Notes, 22 June 2022); the 2024 conference, April 19–21 at the Hyatt Regency O'Hare in Rosemont, closed registration as "the largest conference we've ever had", with more than 200 meetings and workshops from running for local union office to "reviving the strike" (labornotes.org/2024), over 4,700 attending by a participant's count (Washington Socialist), and the Labor Network for Sustainability joined it and ran a Climate Change and Labor meetup there (Labor Network for Sustainability).

The 2026 conference met June 12–14 in Chicago with 300 workshops and panels, sectoral meetings at the heart of each year's conference and a chance for workers "to come together across unions, sectors, and identities" (Labor Notes, 2 July 2026), while the about page still announces it as "Our next conference" (labornotes.org/about), which the census records with the latest story of 29 October 2026 and the footer's 2005-2023: "the about page still announces the June 12-14, 2026 Chicago conference as 'next', so that page is not current" (maryleelabor record).

Its books include A Troublemaker’s Handbook (Dan La Botz, 1991) and Democracy is Power (Mike Parker and Martha Gruelle) (Wikipedia), with A Troublemaker's Handbook 2 among its best-sellers and "tens of thousands of these strategy manuals" sold (labornotes.org/about), a participant reporting many who credit it and Secrets of a Successful Organizer with their organizing (Washington Socialist); with local unions and community groups it organizes Troublemakers Schools (labornotes.org/about), and the census lists these, a podcast and an Archives link it did not read among the holdings and states no count of articles or issues (maryleelabor record).

Wikipedia's article is about the magazine and sends "Labour voucher", the alternative currency, to its own article, and it carries its own notices that it "contains promotional content" and "needs more citations" (April 2025) (Wikipedia); the census finds no stated limits in the saved pages and leaves the archives section, the staff and board page, the writer guidelines and the articles themselves unchecked (maryleelabor record).

By the census it answers how union activists and rank-and-file members describe a named campaign, strike or fight over union democracy and what tactics the rank-and-file current around it recommends, from reporting by staff and contributing writers, books and pamphlets, biennial conferences and Troublemakers Schools, and it is "NOT a strike dataset" (maryleelabor record).

At its name, a new address, on Google AI Mode by the operator's report, signed out, on 31 October 2026, the Capture Registry reads it first innocently, the founding, the headquarters and four lines of work, finds the composition "Faithful, and close to #1725 where it names the caucuses Labor Notes supports", the caucuses carried with "historically supporting factions like the Teamsters for a Democratic Union (TDU)", the project reached by name with its founding, magazine, conference, schools and caucus work, and the founder named (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The registry finds the independence not carried, the about page's "independent publication" and its critique of leaders absent: "The organ that prints criticism of union leadership is the condition #1725 names; the composition gives the magazine's subjects and not its standing" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), and #1725 holds that where composing systems close a dispute "by omission, balance or verdict", the defeated critique "loses its organ, its holder and its route, and so cannot be taken up later" (#1725; labornotes.org/about).
